Cartilaginous Joints

  • In cartilaginous joints, the space between the articulating bony surfaces is filled with a cartilaginous pad.
  • Two types are:

Primary Cartilaginous Joints (Synchondrosis)

Secondary Cartilaginous Joints (Symphysis)
  • Immobile
  • Occur where ossification centres remain separated by hyaline cartilage.
  • Found in bones that form from more than one ossification centre.

  • Slightly mobile

  • Built to handle a variety of stresses (compression, tension, etc.).
  • Permanent and provide limited movement.
  • Found along the midline (e.g., pubic symphysis, intervertebral joints). (Option A and D ruled out)
  • Strong ligaments reinforce the joints and are key to stability and movement.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Intramembranous ossification is the direct formation of bone from mesenchymal tissue without a cartilage precursor.

  • It occurs within highly vascular connective tissue membranes, where mesenchymal cells differentiate into osteoprogenitor cells → osteoblasts, which secrete osteoid that mineralises to form woven bone (primary spongiosa) and later remodels into mature bone.
  • The frontal bone is a classic example, as it is ossified in fibrous mesenchyme from primary ossification centers appearing in early fetal life, which expand and fuse to form the bone.
  • This mechanism is typical of flat bones of the skull.
  • In contrast, most bones develop by endochondral ossification, where a preformed cartilage model is replaced by bone.

Femur (Option A): A long bone that develops by endochondral ossification using a cartilage model.

Tibia (Option C): Another long bone formed by endochondral ossification, not intramembranous.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The muscle demonstrated is the deltoid muscle, the principal abductor of the shoulder from approximately 15° to 90°.
  • While the supraspinatus muscle initiates the first 15° of abduction, the deltoid is responsible for the majority of shoulder abduction thereafter.
  • The deltoid is innervated by the axillary nerve (C5, C6), which passes through the quadrangular space around the surgical neck of the humerus.
  • Axillary nerve injury commonly occurs following fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus or anterior dislocation of the shoulder.
  • Patients present with weakness of shoulder abduction beyond 15°, flattening of the shoulder due to deltoid wasting, and loss of sensation over the "regimental badge" area on the lateral aspect of the shoulder.

Musculocutaneous nerve (Option A) supplies the anterior compartment of the arm, including the biceps brachii, brachialis, and coracobrachialis muscles. Injury results in weak elbow flexion and weakened forearm supination, with sensory loss over the lateral forearm. It does not innervate the deltoid muscle, making it an incorrect option.

Radial nerve (Option C) innervates the extensor muscles of the arm and forearm. Radial nerve injury classically produces wrist drop, finger extension weakness, and sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand. It has no motor supply to the deltoid muscle, and therefore does not explain isolated weakness of shoulder abduction.

Suprascapular nerve (Option D) supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. The supraspinatus initiates the first 15° of shoulder abduction, while the infraspinatus contributes to external rotation of the shoulder. Although injury to this nerve affects the initiation of abduction, the deltoid muscle itself is supplied by the axillary nerve, making this option incorrect.

The neck-shaft angle (angle of inclination) is the angle between the axis of the femoral neck and the longitudinal axis of the femoral shaft.

  • It is essential for optimal hip joint mechanics and muscle leverage.
  • In adults, the angle averages approximately 125° (range 120°-135°).
  • This configuration allows efficient transmission of body weight and maintains proper alignment of the hip joint.
  • At birth, the angle is higher (coxa valga) and gradually decreases to adult values with growth.
  • A decrease below 120° is termed coxa vara, which leads to limb shortening and may result in a Trendelenburg gait due to altered biomechanics.
  • An increase above 135° is termed coxa valga, which alters hip joint mechanics and may predispose to instability.

90° (Option A): Too acute; represents a severe abnormality of the neck-shaft angle and is not compatible with normal hip biomechanics.

110° (Option B): Below normal range; falls into the coxa vara spectrum.

150° (Option D): Above normal range; falls into the coxa valga spectrum.

  • Clinically, the short external rotators (piriformis, obturator internus, gemelli, quadratus femoris) provide dynamic stability to the hip joint, particularly in controlling femoral head position during movement.

Obturator internus (Option B): A primary external rotator, part of the short lateral rotator group that stabilizes the hip.

Quadratus femoris (Option C): A strong lateral rotator of the hip and an important stabilizer of the femoral head.

The sciatic nerve (L4-S3) is the largest branch of the sacral plexus and supplies the principal muscles of the posterior thigh, including semimembranosus, semitendinosus, the long head of biceps femoris, and the ischial (hamstring) part of adductor magnus.

  • After leaving the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, it descends deep in the gluteal region and into the posterior thigh, where it gives muscular branches to these hamstring-related muscles.
  • Gluteus maximus is not innervated by the sciatic nerve; it is supplied separately by the inferior gluteal nerve.
  • This distinction is clinically important because sciatic nerve lesions weaken knee flexion and distal leg function, whereas inferior gluteal nerve injury primarily impairs powerful hip extension, such as rising from sitting or climbing stairs.

  • The adductor magnus has dual innervation:
    • Adductor (pubofemoral) portion receives fibres from the posterior branch of the obturator nerve.
    • Hamstring (ischiocondylar) portion is supplied by the tibial component of the sciatic nerve.
  • This explains why only the posterior division of the obturator nerve contributes its obturator innervation.

Anterior division only (Option A): The anterior division mainly supplies adductor longus, gracilis, and usually adductor brevis, but not adductor magnus.

The saphenous nerve is the most likely injured nerve because it is the terminal purely sensory branch of the femoral nerve and runs through the adductor canal before becoming subcutaneous between the tendons of sartorius and gracilis.

  • Because it carries no motor fibres, injury causes sensory loss such as numbness, tingling, or paresthesia without muscle weakness.
  • The nerve is particularly vulnerable in procedures involving the adductor canal, medial knee surgery, and vein harvesting due to its close anatomical relationship to the femoral vessels in this region.

Sural nerve (Option A): The sural nerve supplies the posterolateral leg and lateral side of the foot, not the medial leg.

Tibial nerve (Option C): Tibial nerve injury causes sensory loss over the sole of the foot and motor weakness in plantar flexion, not isolated medial leg numbness.

question: A patient complains of numbness along the medial aspect of the leg extending to the medial border of the foot after surgery in the adductor canal. Which nerve is most likely injured?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The femoral nerve is most likely compressed.

  • It arises from L2-L4 roots and descends through psoas major, making it vulnerable to compression by retroperitoneal haemorrhage.
  • The femoral nerve supplies the quadriceps femoris, the principal extensor of the knee; therefore, injury causes marked weakness of knee extension.
  • Loss of the patellar reflex (L2-L4) is a classic sign because this reflex depends on intact femoral nerve conduction.
  • Sensory loss over the anterior thigh occurs due to involvement of its anterior cutaneous branches, and medial leg sensory loss may also occur if the saphenous branch is affected.
  • Clinically, femoral neuropathy often presents with quadriceps wasting, knee buckling, and difficulty climbing stairs or rising from a seated position.

Obturator nerve (Option B): Obturator nerve lesions mainly cause weakness of thigh adduction and sensory loss over the medial thigh, without loss of knee extension or absent patellar reflex.

Sciatic nerve (Option C): Sciatic nerve injury affects the posterior thigh and muscles below the knee, causing weakness of knee flexion and distal leg deficits rather than isolated anterior thigh sensory loss.

question: A dry femur specimen is shown with a marked roughened area in the given image. What is the primary action of this muscle attached here at the hip joint?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The gluteus medius is the most powerful abductor of the hip joint, acting along with gluteus minimus as the primary muscles responsible for hip abduction.

  • It arises from the outer surface of the ilium between the iliac crest and posterior gluteal line above, and the anterior gluteal line below, and inserts onto the lateral surface of the greater trochanter, providing an effective mechanical advantage for abduction.
  • In addition to abduction, the anterior fibers of gluteus medius produce medial rotation of the hip.
  • During the single-leg stance phase of gait, it plays a critical role in maintaining pelvic stability, preventing the pelvis from sagging on the unsupported side.
  • Weakness or paralysis leads to a positive Trendelenburg sign and a lurching (Trendelenburg) gait.

  • Although several muscles assist in abduction, such as gluteus minimus, tensor fascia lata, piriformis, and sartorius, they are not as powerful as gluteus medius.

Gluteus maximus (Option A): Primarily a powerful extensor and lateral rotator of the hip, not a major abductor.

Tensor fascia lata (Option C): Assists in abduction and medial rotation, but is not the most powerful abductor.

Piriformis (Option D): Primarily a lateral rotator of the hip; it assists in abduction mainly when the hip is flexed, and is not the most powerful abductor.

The blastocyst implants in the functional layer of the uterine endometrium 6-7 days after fertilization. This corresponds to days 20-22 of a standard menstrual cycle.

  • Secretory phase: 3 layers can be recognized in the endometrium:
    • Stratum compactum
    • Stratum spongiosum
    • Stratum basale
  • The first two layers (stratum compactum and spongiosum) are together known as the stratum functionale or the functional layer.
  • If implantation does not occur, the functional layer is shed off during menstruation.
  • If implantation occurs, the functional layer is retained as the decidua.

Timeline of Pre-embryonic Phase Development (1st two weeks)

  • < 24 hrs: Zygote is formed; cleavage begins immediately
  • 2 to 3 days: 5-8 cell stage
  • Timeline of implantation:
    • 3-4 days after fertilization: Morula (12-16 cells) enters the uterus.
    • 4th day after fertilization: Advanced morula reaches the uterine lumen.
    • 4-5 days after fertilization: Early blastocyst stage is seen.
    • 5 to 6 days: Zona pellucida disappears
    • 6-7 days after fertilization: Blastocyst implants in the uterus. Implantation corresponds to 20-22 days of the menstrual cycle.
  • 9 days: Bilaminar disc formation
  • 12 days: Formation of extraembryonic mesoderm.

Chronological order of events in the pre-embryonic phase is fertilization, followed by cleavage (formation of blastomeres), compaction (at the 8-cell stage), cavitation (formation of the blastocyst), and finally implantation into the uterine endometrium.

Events of the pre-embryonic phase of development:

  • Fertilization
  • Cleavage - Formation of blastomeres; the cells are loosely arranged until the 8-cell stage.
  • Compaction - After 3 cleavages, the blastomeres are held together by tight junctions.
  • Differentiation - The compacted 8-cell stage divides to form a 16-cell morula.
  • Cavitation - Formation of the blastocyst with inner cell and outer cell mass.
  • Hatching of the blastocyst - Release of the blastocyst from the zona pellucida.
  • Implantation - Attachment of the developing embryo to the uterine endometrium.
  • Cell mass differentiation - Differentiation of the embryoblast (inner cell mass) into columnar epiblast cells and cuboidal hypoblast cells.

Option C: Umblical vein and IVC

  • The umblical vein is connected to the IVC via ductus venosus.

Ductus venosus:

  • Fetal circulation is unlike adult circulation, which uses physiological shunts to carry oxygenated blood to tissues and bypass developing organs.
  • The fetus's viability heavily relies on these shunts to adequately perfuse developing tissues and organs, especially the brain and heart.
  • The ductus venosus is a shunt that allows oxygenated blood in the umbilical vein to bypass the liver and is essential for normal fetal circulation.
  • Blood becomes oxygenated in the placenta and travels to the right atrium via umbilical veins through the ductus venosus, then to the inferior vena cava.
  • This oxygenated blood then passes through the foramen ovale, an opening between the atria, into the left atrium to be distributed systemically.
  • Therefore, the ductus venosus plays a crucial role in maintaining this unique circulation pattern.
  • Fetal circulation studies are done via Doppler ultrasound or MRI to ensure proper blood flow through these shunts.
  • The impedance or absence of flow through these shunts may correlate with aneuploidies, cardiac defects, and/or other postpartum disease states.
  • Postpartum, the ductus venosus closed, secondary to increased cardiac pressures and decreased circulating prostaglandins.
  • The ductus venosus is critical for proper fetal circulation.
  • Still, disruption of flow in utero or failure to close this shunt postpartum can lead to adverse antenatal and perinatal outcomes.

Fig.: Fetal circulation

  • There is no structure that connects the descending aorta with the pulmonary trunk

Option B: Right atrium and left atrium

  • The right and left atriums are connected through the foramen ovale.

The clavicle is classified as a modified long bone because, although it has a shaft and two ends, it shows several structural and developmental differences from typical long bones.

The Haversian system (osteon) is the fundamental structural and functional unit of compact (cortical) bone.

  • It is a cylindrical structure composed of concentric lamellae arranged around a central Haversian canal, which contains blood vessels and nerve fibers.
  • Osteons are typically oriented parallel to the long axis of the bone, especially in long bones, providing maximum resistance to mechanical stress.
  • Each osteon is bounded by a cement line, distinguishing it from adjacent osteons.
  • The Haversian canals are interconnected by Volkmann’s canals, which run transversely or obliquely, allowing communication between adjacent osteons and linking them to the periosteum and medullary cavity.
  • Within the lamellae are lacunae containing osteocytes, interconnected by canaliculi, forming a microscopic network that enables diffusion of nutrients and waste products, ensuring that no osteocyte is far from a blood supply.

In contrast, cancellous (spongy) bone (Option A) is composed of a trabecular network of lamellae and lacks true Haversian systems, although it remains highly vascular through marrow spaces.

To stabilize the elbow joint (Option C): Elbow stability is unrelated to humeral rotation at the shoulder.

To assist medial rotation (Option D): Lateral and medial rotations are opposite actions.
